chunk_findings.detail: The new branch decides to surface `export_refresh` by truthiness rather than by presence: `if (... and out.data.get("export_refresh") and "export_refresh" not in payload_key)`. The comment right below states the intended contract — the key is "absent when nothing was refreshed" and merge/complete carry it "as the CLI's `--json` does". A truthiness test conflates "the key is absent" with "the key is present but falsy". If a refresh runs but changes nothing (the value is an empty list/dict) or otherwise serialises to a falsy value, `out.data.get("export_refresh")` is falsy, `export_refresh` is not appended to `payload_key`, and the MCP response omits the field — while the CLI `--json` path emits it. A client then cannot distinguish "refresh ran, nothing changed" from "no refresh happened", which is exactly the distinction the field exists to convey. The guard should test presence (`"export_refresh" in out.data`) rather than truthiness. (I cannot confirm from this part that the field can in fact be present-but-falsy, so this is flagged as a correctness risk in the stated contract rather than a demonstrated crash.)

chunk_findings.detail:
`_export_section()` locates the end of the "## Exporting documents" section with `re.search(r"^## ", README[start + 5:], flags=re.M)`, which does not skip fenced code blocks. This change's own intent states the README section includes "a worked example of customising the changelog template"; a rendered changelog example is markdown and contains heading lines such as `## [1.2.3] - 2026-10-02`. Given a README whose export section contains

    ```
    ## [1.2.3] - 2026-10-02
    ```

the search stops at that fenced line, so `_export_section()` returns only the text up to it. Any kind name, default target, `ddflow export <verb>` occurrence, or stale phrase that sits after that line is never inspected: `test_every_export_kind_is_documented_in_the_readme_and_the_help_topic`, `test_every_export_flag_and_verb_the_docs_name_exists` (the reverse-verb asserts) and `test_no_export_doc_says_a_shipped_feature_is_not_done_yet` will then pass without actually checking the tail of the section (or fail spuriously if the expected content is after the fence). The helper should skip fenced regions (or match only `^## ` outside fences) before taking the boundary.

chunk_findings.detail: The sentence is an ordered identity, not a bag of names: "the command and MCP tool are A and B" asserts command=A, MCP tool=B. Here A is `api/export.py` and B is `surfaces/commands/export.py`, so as written the CLI command is claimed to live in `api/export.py` and the MCP tool in `surfaces/commands/export.py`. That is inverted relative to the paths themselves — a directory literally named `surfaces/commands/` holds the command surface, and the `api/` module is the tool surface the MCP server calls. A developer following the docstring to change the `export` command will open `api/export.py`, and one looking for the MCP tool will open `surfaces/commands/export.py`; both land on the wrong file. The correct text is "the MCP tool and command are ``api/export.py`` and ``surfaces/commands/export.py``" (equivalently, list `surfaces/commands/export.py` first after the word "command").

chunk_findings.detail: The forward verb check enumerates a fixed set of five verbs, so it does not actually enforce the guarantee the test advertises. Given a span scraped by `_export_spans`, if the docs name any verb outside `(enable|disable|ack|eject|validate)` that is not in `X.VERBS`, the `re.match` returns `None`, the `if m and ...` guard is skipped, `bad` stays empty, and the test passes. Concrete input: put the line `` `ddflow export list` `` (or `ddflow export refresh`) in the README "Exporting documents" section and/or `ddflow/templates/prompts/help/export.md`. `_export_spans` yields `"ddflow export list"`, no flags are found, the verb regex does not match `list`, and the test succeeds even though `ddflow export list` is not a real verb in `X.VERBS` — exactly the kind of stale/aspirational doc text the test is meant to reject (the reverse loop then also never notices, since `list` is not a key of `X.VERBS`). Matching a capture like `ddflow export ([a-z][a-z-]*)` and conditionally checking the captured token against `X.VERBS` would close this.
